chunks: A man from Banu Hashim wrote to Abu Ja'far (the second Imam), peace be upon him: 'I had made a vow for several years to go out to a coast from the coasts of the sea to our region, where the volunteers were stationed, similar to their stations in Jeddah and other coasts of the sea. Do you think, may I be your ransom, that I am obliged to fulfill it, or not? Or should I redeem the going out to that place with something from the doors of righteousness, so that I may go to it, if God wills?' He wrote to him in his own hand: 'And I read it. If one of the opposing party heard your vow from you, then fulfillment is obligatory upon you, if you fear a disgrace; otherwise, spend what you intended to spend on that in the doors of righteousness. May God grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.'

key_terms.أَبْوَابُ اَلْبِرِّ: Doors of righteousness (channels of charity and good deeds)
key_terms.اَلْمُخَالِفُونَ: The opposing party (often referring to enemies or rivals)
key_terms.فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a term of respect)
key_terms.نَذْرٌ: A vow or promise to perform an act of worship or good deed

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fulfilling a vow to go to the coast for jihad if no one heard it?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) highlights the jurisprudential nuance of 'conditional vows' in Shia fiqh, where the presence of an opposing party (al-mukhalifun) transforms a voluntary vow into an obligatory one to prevent them from gaining spiritual or social advantage. The Imam’s instruction to redirect funds to the 'doors of righteousness' if the vow is not strictly binding underscores the flexibility of nathr (vows) and the priority of sincere intention over rigid formalism when no external pressure exists.
